solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicatorNotes.receiving: whoever receives something takes it in, so the word for modest takes the promotion inside itself

annotation.surface: A prim person is accused of decadence for accepting a promotion at work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Is modest' reads as a description of the degenerate, but the whole phrase is the outer word; 'promotion' is advertising, not a rise in rank.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe someone sunk in moral decline and self-indulgence.

indicatorNotes.to comprehend: comprehend has an older sense, to include or contain, so the attempts hold British inside them

annotation.surface: Someone tries to understand the old clans of Britain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Comprehend' looks like understanding, but here it means include, its older sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are groups bound by kinship and a common ancestor.

entries.clue: Rest cue round centre of black (9)

indicatorNotes.round: one word goes round another, encircling it, so the prompt wraps the single letter
indicatorNotes.centre of: the centre of a five-letter word is its third letter, the one in the middle

blocks.note: a cue prompts memory, as a prompt does

annotation.surface: A snooker player rests the cue while going for the black ball.
annotation.walkthrough: The snooker picture of rest, cue and black is all misdirection: 'Rest' is the definition, not the cue support, and 'cue' means a prompt.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what is left over after a part is taken away.

indicatorNotes.purchasing: to purchase is to acquire and hold, so the phrase before it has got the answer in its grip

blocks.note: the answer starts at the fifth letter of the first word and runs over the gap into the second

annotation.surface: A shopper spends more than planned when buying a necklace.
annotation.walkthrough: The spending story makes 'purchasing' look literal; it only means the first two words hold the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose fit: strictly the hanging ornament on a chain, but commonly the whole piece worn round the neck.

indicatorNotes.going topless: in a down clue the top is the first letter, and going without it removes that letter

annotation.surface: More trouble arises when someone goes topless in public.
annotation.walkthrough: 'More trouble' reads as a phrase, but 'More' alone is the definition, as in 'bring some other chairs'.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective sense of additional, further: 'some other ideas' means some more ideas.

blocks.note: close weather is stuffy, without fresh air

annotation.surface: A barber promises a hard, close shave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close shaven' looks like one phrase, but 'close' is stuffy weather; the question mark flags that shaving is only one way to lose hair.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: shaving is one way to end up bald, hence the question mark.

indicatorNotes.taking: taking something in means holding it, so the letters for exercise take the breather inside them

annotation.surface: A gym session is dropped in favour of a rest, running on into 14 down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breather' suggests a pause, but here it is the organ that breathes. The ellipsis joins the surface to 14 down; the clues solve separately.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sudden fall, as when prices go down steeply.

blocks.note: a term of endearment for a loved one
costly, too high in price, in British usage

annotation.surface: A warning that a lover might be too much.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain the answer also means costly, which is the sense that fits excessive prices.
annotation.definitionFit: One word, two senses: a beloved person, and overpriced in everyday British speech.

indicatorNotes.catching: to catch something is to trap and hold it, so the word for match holds the U

blocks.note: to tally is to match up
U = United, as in team names

annotation.surface: A football match ends level after United score at the last.
annotation.walkthrough: Level, match and United all read as football; each is a plain abbreviation or synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: at last, after a long wait.

indicatorNotes.covered in: something covered in a coating sits inside it, so the fat wraps around the pig

annotation.surface: A pig is left lying in its own fat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as a verb, abandoned, but it is the side of a ship; this is the old name for port.
annotation.definitionFit: A nautical sense: the left-hand side of a ship looking forward, now called port.

entries.clue: Task Queen performed before do’s opening (6)

indicatorNotes.before: before means ahead of, so the queen and the verb come ahead of the last letter
indicatorNotes.opening: a word's opening is its start, its first letter

blocks.note: to run a show is to perform it

annotation.surface: The Queen performs a duty at the start of a party.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'do' is British slang for a party, which is what makes the royal scene work.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a short trip to do a small job.

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the song goes around the word for popular

blocks.note: a shanty is one kind of sailors' song

annotation.surface: A popular shanty about an old salt, a veteran sailor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Salt' reads as a sailor, fitting the shanty, but it is the condiment; the question mark flags salt as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: salt is one thing added to food for flavour, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: First Lady in France creating excitement (5)

indicatorNotes.in: one thing in another sits inside it, so the first woman sits inside the letters for France

annotation.surface: A president's wife visiting France causes a stir.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a president's wife, but it is the first woman in the Bible.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a feverish state of nervous excitement, as in 'World Cup fever'.

indicatorNotes.taking: taking something in means holding it, so the balance takes the exercise inside it

blocks.note: the rest = the balance, what remains

annotation.surface: Continuing 7 down: self-control means balancing exercise with rest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Balance' suggests poise, but it is the remainder, as on a bill. The ellipsis links the surface from 7 down only.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: holding oneself or something else in check.

entries.clue: Trudged and ran holding in stomach (7)

indicatorNotes.holding in: to hold something in is to keep it inside, so the running word keeps the stomach inside

annotation.surface: A walker trudges and runs while sucking in their stomach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Holding in stomach' reads as a posture, but 'holding in' is the container signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A less common sense: to walk with heavy, stiff steps, as if on stumps.

entries.clue: Enthusiastic over capital line in song (8)

indicatorNotes.over: over means above, and in a down clue the upper piece comes first

annotation.surface: Someone enthuses over a great line in a song.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' reads as excellent, the old British sense, but it is a capital city.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: an unaccompanied part-song for several voices, popular in the Renaissance.

indicatorNotes.covering: a cover goes over and around a thing, so the needling word wraps the L

blocks.note: to needle someone is to tease them

annotation.surface: Pine needles lie over big plants.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Needles' looks like a plural noun but is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: prickly plants whose dried heads were once used to raise the nap on cloth.

indicatorNotes.under: under means below, and in a down clue the lower piece comes second
indicatorNotes.leader: the leader goes at the front, so it is the first letter

annotation.surface: A political party suffers under a leader in decline.
annotation.walkthrough: Labour is the British left-wing party; 'Labour's leader' looks like a politician but gives only its first letter, and the final 's is 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a verb: to weaken or waste away.

entries.clue: Demure gal I admire pinching finery (7)

indicatorNotes.pinching: to pinch is to steal, and the phrase has stolen the answer and keeps it within

blocks.note: the answer starts in the last two letters of the first word and ends on the first letter of the last, spanning four words

annotation.surface: A modest girl is caught stealing fancy clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: The shoplifting story makes 'pinching' literal; it only says the answer sits inside the words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: ceremonial robes and insignia, fine dress generally.

indicatorNotes.embracing: an embrace wraps arms around someone, so the blokes wrap around the letter
indicatorNotes.heart: the heart of a word is its middle

annotation.surface: The men hugging a girlfriend rile others, the story running on into 22 across.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sweetheart' looks like a lover but is split: the heart of SWEET.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose sense: to lead someone to act is to prompt or provoke them.

blocks.note: the surface reading: a coat or jacket for dogs
the setter's reading: canines are pointed teeth, and the question is what coats a tooth

annotation.surface: A dog coat for the family pet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Canines' suggests dogs, but canines are also teeth, and enamel is their hard outer coat.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the hard outer layer that shields every tooth, canines included.

entries.clue: … feeling thrilled with sex embracing blokes (9)

indicatorNotes.with: with means alongside, so the thrilled word is followed by the rest
indicatorNotes.embracing: an embrace wraps arms around someone, so the word for sex wraps around the blokes

annotation.surface: Continuing 20 across, someone is excited by sex with men.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' for sex appeal is an old crossword standby. The ellipsis joins the surface from 20 across only.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an emotion or attitude held about something.

indicatorNotes.on: on means placed upon, and in a down clue the upper piece comes first

blocks.note: a coaster is a drinks mat
the Ure is a Yorkshire river

annotation.surface: A coastal ship is getting on a river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coaster' suggests a ship but is a drinks mat. The Ure is a river in Yorkshire, England.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'getting on' means ageing, and the answer as an adjective means grown older.
annotation.definitionNote: 'Getting on' is an idiomatic phrase for being no longer young.

indicatorNotes.going up and down: in a down clue the word reads the same going upwards as going downwards

blocks.note: the answer is the same read either way up the grid

annotation.surface: A canoe bobbing on the waves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up and down' looks like bobbing on water, but it says the answer reads the same both ways in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: a covered canoe first built by Inuit hunters.

indicatorNotes.back: going back means going in the other direction, so the creature is read right to left

annotation.surface: An animal's back reveals a plate of bone, like an armadillo's.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Creature's back' looks like the anatomy the definition describes, but 'back' is the reversal signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical term: a thin layer or plate, used in anatomy for part of a vertebra.

annotation.surface: A pot is chosen to suit a plant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Container' is a word in the charade here, not a signal to put one piece inside another.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: a spiny Mediterranean plant whose leaves decorate Corinthian columns.

indicatorNotes.flipping: to flip something is to turn it over, so the word for mocks is turned end to end

blocks.note: to ape is to mock by imitation

annotation.surface: Someone scorns a spouse's maintenance payments in a divorce.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' could be a mild British curse, fitting the bitter surface, but it is the reversal signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a formal parting of a married couple, often the step before or instead of divorce.

indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so take the start of each word

blocks.note: the first letters of the four words

annotation.surface: A description of an impulsive act.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer and also spells it with its first letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes acting without thought, which is what the word means.
